Title: Aim Your Knee at Your Little Toe Until the Wheel Stands Up
Description: Your skate rolling inward is not fixed by tightening anything. A certified coach's cue is a direction: push your supporting knee slightly forward and outward, toward your little toe, until the wheel underneath is standing completely upright. Practise it while scooting — one leg supporting on a centre edge, the other pushing continuously, like a scooter. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.
Keywords: inline skate pronation fix, centre edge skating, scooting drill rollerblading, ankle collapse skates

Title: Point Your Trailing Foot Like a Ballerina
Description: The second drill of a certified coach's pronation routine holds a centre edge for longer than scooting does. Sink into a deep front knee bend, kneecap over your toes, then point your trailing back foot like a ballerina into a toe roll. Keep nudging the front knee toward your little toes, or the skate collapses onto its inside edge again. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.
Keywords: toe roll drill inline skating, one leg glide rollerblade, skating balance drills, inside edge collapse

Title: Hold the Glide for Four Metres, Then Make It Shorter
Description: The drill that turns a bouncy stride into a smooth one is done in slow motion. Push out on one foot, regroup into a tight parallel stance, then pause there on a centre edge for four to five metres before the next push. As your balance improves, shorten the pause a little at a time, until it matches the natural tempo of push and glide. The pause is the lesson, not the delay. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.
Keywords: slow motion skating drill, inline skating stride, how to glide longer on skates, rollerblading technique

Title: Sore Feet: Two Causes, and Only One Is the Boot
Description: Bad-quality skates hurt whether new or not, a rigid shell always produces some pain, and most beginner foot pain is a fitting problem in disguise — Cass. But a certified coach names a second cause, nothing to do with the boot: the muscles of the feet and ankles are weak, and skating demands intense use of them. Two causes, two fixes. From ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.
Keywords: sore feet after skating, roller skate foot pain, skate fitting problems, foot strength for skaters

Title: Tension You Leave in Your Feet Settles There
Description: A certified coach names a cause of foot discomfort that is not about strength: tension picked up during the session, then left to settle in the feet because nothing works it out afterwards. Her routine strengthens and stretches feet and ankles in the same movements — training balance while it does — then ends with soothing manipulation. It is an after, not a warm-up. From ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.
Keywords: post skate stretches, foot exercises for skaters, ankle strength skating, skating recovery routine

Title: The Cheapest Thing in a Skater's Bag Is a Ball
Description: A certified coach ends her foot routine with a massage or myofascial ball rolled under the foot, to release the tension left by skating and to promote circulation. It costs less than anything else you own for skating, it lives in a bag, and it is used after the session rather than before. Nothing about it fixes a badly fitting boot — that is a separate problem with a separate answer. From ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.
Keywords: massage ball feet, myofascial release skaters, tired feet after skating, skate recovery

Title: A Stiff Lower Back After Skating May Be Your Sides
Description: The place that aches is not always the place at fault. A certified coach points at the side body — the muscles down the flanks that are hard to reach and easy to ignore — and says that weakness or tightness there can contribute to lower back pain. Which means the useful thing to stretch after a long skate may not be your back at all. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.
Keywords: lower back pain skating, side body stretch, skating fitness, stretches for skaters

Title: You Can Stretch Your Sides Without Taking the Skates Off
Description: A certified coach's side body class is done on skates, while rolling. Simple movements reach the flank muscles that are hard to get at standing still, and they strengthen those muscles at the same time, because the skate is moving underneath you. Done at the end of a session rather than the start, it is aimed at the stiffness you are about to feel, not the one you already have. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.
Keywords: stretching on skates, on skates fitness class, roller skating warm down, side stretch rollerblading

Title: Your Head Is Ready Before Your Body Is
Description: Coming back after a fall, the split is normal: your mind is excited to skate again while your body still remembers the impact, and hesitation is a completely natural reaction. A certified coach's advice is to stop comparing yourself to how you skated before. Muscle memory comes back fast. What needs time is the nervous system reconvincing itself that rolling on wheels is safe. From ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.
Keywords: skating after a fall, lost confidence skating, returning to roller skating, fear of falling skates

Title: Come Back a Better Skater Than the One Who Fell
Description: A certified coach treats a comeback as an opening, not a loss. Go back to beginner drills — balance, posture, stopping — and use the time to fix old habits and learn the stops you rushed past. Keep sessions shorter and better, and honour any hesitation your body shows: those limits are information. Pain that persists is a question for a professional, not a skating account. From ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.
Keywords: returning to skating after injury, beginner skating drills, roller skating confidence, learning to stop on skates
